summary: Lays out architectural principles for a quantum internet, a network that lets distant nodes share quantum entanglement. It explains how a quantum network stack differs from the classical one and sketches the building blocks, such as repeaters and entangled pairs. It is an informational framework, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine two friends with magic coins that always land the same way, even far apart. This document is a plan for building a network that links such magic coins across the whole world.

what is quantum entanglement in networking
how does quantum entanglement work in networks
subtitle: A framework for networks that distribute quantum entanglement between distant nodes.

tldr.problem: Quantum networks have fundamentally different properties from classical networks, yet there is no framework for how to organize and manage them. The first quantum entanglement networks have been realized, but lack practical design principles.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC introduces architectural principles for a quantum internet built on distributing entangled qubit pairs called Bell pairs. It explains how quantum repeaters use entanglement swapping to extend entangled pairs across long distances, and outlines design goals such as supporting diverse hardware, managing fidelity as a resource, and minimizing memory idle time.
tldr.outcome: This is an informational framework from the Quantum Internet Research Group to guide first-generation quantum networks. It does not specify a protocol, but rather establishes design thinking for an era when quantum and classical networks will hybrid together.

today: RFC 9340 is an informational framework that has not been obsoleted. It represents the consensus of the Quantum Internet Research Group and serves as a foundation for ongoing research and standards development. The first fully quantum multinode networks have been demonstrated in laboratory settings, and quantum key distribution networks at metropolitan scales are commercially available.

sections.title: What Is a Quantum Network
sections.content:
A quantum network uses quantum mechanical phenomena to achieve capabilities that classical networks cannot. Instead of sending bits between computers, a quantum network distributes entangled qubits -- quantum bits that share a strange correlation where measuring one instantly affects the other, regardless of distance.

The most famous application is quantum key distribution (QKD), which creates unbreakable encryption keys by relying on the laws of physics rather than mathematical difficulty. Quantum networks also enable distributed quantum computing, where multiple quantum computers work together on a single problem, and quantum-enhanced sensing networks that measure physical quantities with unprecedented precision.

Today's quantum networks are in their infancy -- comparable to classical networks in the 1960s, when engineers manually configured hardware-specific interfaces rather than having a network stack. This RFC provides design guidance for the next generation.
sections.plainLanguage: A quantum network is like having a pair of magic coins at two different locations that always match when flipped. Instead of sending messages, the network sends these magic coins so distant computers can share secrets or work together.

sections.title: Qubits and Entanglement
sections.content:
A qubit (quantum bit) is the quantum version of a classical bit. Unlike a classical bit that must be either 0 or 1, a qubit can exist in superposition -- a combination of both states at once, described by probability amplitudes. When measured, the qubit collapses into 0 or 1, but until then it behaves like both simultaneously.

Two or more qubits can become entangled, a state where their properties are correlated in ways that have no classical equivalent. A Bell pair is the simplest entangled state: two qubits with perfect correlations such that measuring one always produces the opposite or the same outcome as the other, even across vast distances. Importantly, entanglement cannot be shared -- if two qubits are maximally entangled, neither can be entangled with a third qubit, making it inherently private.

A quantum network distributes Bell pairs as its fundamental resource. Applications like QKD simply measure both qubits to obtain shared random bits that serve as encryption keys. More complex applications build quantum gates and computations on top of entangled pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: A qubit is like a spinning coin that hasn't landed yet -- it's kind of both heads and tails at the same time. When two qubits are entangled, they are like magic coins that always match, even far apart. The network's job is to create and send these magic coin pairs between distant nodes.

sections.title: Achieving Quantum Connectivity
sections.content:
Creating entanglement over long distances faces four fundamental challenges. First, measuring a qubit destroys its superposition and entanglement, so error detection and correction must work without reading the qubit. Second, the no-cloning theorem forbids copying unknown quantum states, so traditional signal amplification is impossible. Third, even tiny environmental noise (called decoherence) degrades the quality of qubits, measured by a quantity called fidelity (where 1.0 is perfect). Fourth, transmitting qubits directly over long distances is extremely inefficient beyond a few tens of kilometers.

The solution is entanglement swapping using quantum repeaters. A repeater holds entangled pairs on two adjacent links (A-repeater and repeater-B), then performs a Bell state measurement that consumes both pairs to create a new entangled pair between the distant ends (A-B). This process can be chained across many repeaters to build long-distance entanglement. Errors accumulate at each step, so intermediate nodes perform entanglement distillation to improve fidelity by sacrificing some pairs to test and purify others. Three generations of quantum networks are defined by their error management schemes: first-generation uses distillation, second-generation adds quantum error correction, and third-generation eliminates classical signalling overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: To send magic coins across the world, you set up repeater stations that each have pairs of magic coins. Each station takes its two pairs and creates a new pair linking the distant endpoints. It takes many attempts because of noise, and some pairs must be sacrificed to test that others are good enough.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Elements
sections.content:
A quantum network separates control and data planes, with two parallel data planes: classical (for traditional packets) and quantum (for entangled pairs). Unlike classical networks where a packet carries both user data and headers, quantum data is pure entanglement with no headers -- all control information travels on classical channels and is correlated with qubits by their position in quantum memory.

The network has several types of nodes: quantum routers participate in network control and decide which qubits to swap; automated quantum nodes perform only swapping without control functions; end nodes request and use entangled pairs but need not perform swaps; and non-quantum nodes handle only classical traffic. Quantum links create entanglement on adjacent quantum repeaters, while classical links carry all control traffic.

Physical constraints shape the design. Qubits in memory degrade over seconds due to decoherence. Entanglement generation is slow (currently around 10 Hz) and requires many retries. Only a subset of qubits, called communication qubits, can generate entanglement; a repeater with one communication qubit must generate pairs sequentially over its two links. Finally, different hardware platforms (optical, trapped-ion, nitrogen-vacancy centers) excel at different tasks and will need to interoperate, requiring conversion between incompatible quantum states.
sections.plainLanguage: The quantum network has two separate roads: one for normal messages (classical) and one for magic coins (quantum). Repeater stations are like post offices that receive pairs of magic coins, create new pairs between distant locations, and guide each coin to the right place. Each repeater can only create one new pair at a time, and coins fade after a few seconds, so everything must happen quickly.

sections.title: Architectural Principles
sections.content:
Six key goals guide quantum network design. First, the network must support distributed quantum applications, not just transmit arbitrary quantum states. Second, it must embrace change: a quantum internet should avoid forcing flag-day upgrades like IPv4 to IPv6. Third, it should support heterogeneous hardware platforms, since different technologies have different strengths. Fourth, it must ensure security at the network level, protecting against hijacking or measurement attacks that disrupt QKD. Fifth, networks must be easy to monitor using statistical measures like tomography, since individual qubits cannot be read. Sixth, quantum networks must be resilient to failures of both quantum and classical channels.

Five design principles flow from these goals. Entanglement is the fundamental service. Bell pairs are indistinguishable to applications -- any two pairs of sufficient fidelity are equivalent, enabling flexible resource allocation. Fidelity is part of the service contract between applications and the network -- the network balances cost and quality based on application requirements. Time is an expensive resource due to short memory lifetimes, so minimizing qubit idle time is critical. Finally, the architecture must remain flexible across current and future hardware capabilities, functioning under today's constraints while not blocking tomorrow's improvements.
sections.plainLanguage: Good quantum networks should work with many types of hardware, improve over time without breaking everything, keep secrets safe, and never waste the precious seconds that magic coins stay fresh. The network's job is to deliver reliable pairs at the quality each application needs, not to transmit raw data like classical networks do.

sections.title: Status and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 9340 is an informational document produced by the Quantum Internet Research Group (QIRG), not a protocol specification. It represents consensus on architectural principles from both quantum physics experts and network engineers. The document explicitly states it is not a conclusive statement about how quantum networks will be implemented, but rather a framework to guide discussion and early implementations.

No concrete protocol mechanisms are defined -- the RFC is a thinking document that establishes shared vocabulary and design philosophy. For example, Section 7 sketches a thought experiment inspired by MPLS (label-switched paths for quantum networks) to show what components might be necessary, but this is not a proposal. The quantum internet remains in the research phase, with the first fully quantum multinode network demonstrated in a laboratory setting in 2021. This RFC will likely evolve as deployments mature.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a set of guidelines, not a recipe. It says what quantum networks should aim for and how to think about designing them, but doesn't specify the exact steps. Real quantum networks are still mostly in labs, and this RFC will be updated as they grow.
